title: Excellence in all things
hookLine: a blade being sharpened, and the odd place a hadith chose to talk about excellence

cards: Where would you expect a teaching on excellence? A prayer hall, maybe, or a workshop. Not a blade being sharpened for an animal about to become a family's meal.
But that's where the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, chose to put it. In Sahih Muslim, Shaddad ibn Aws reports him saying, in paraphrase: Allah has prescribed ihsan, excellence, in all things.
So when you kill, kill well, and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare the animal suffering.

teach.b: Ihsan is doing a thing beautifully, doing it well. In the hadith of Jibril, in Sahih Muslim, it's described as worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you.
Today's hadith carries it out of the prayer hall. First, the verb.

The hadith says Allah kataba ihsan: wrote it, prescribed it, the same verb as in the fasting verse of al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "Fasting is prescribed for you." So excellence isn't extra credit. It's written in.
Second, the example. Of everything the hadith could have picked, it picks a moment where cutting corners costs someone who can't complain.

teach.h: CARE FOR THE ONE WITH NO VOICE.
teach.b: Excellence here means care for the one with no voice: a sharp blade, no drawn-out pain. Third, the reach: in all things.
If slaughter can be done with ihsan, so can a spreadsheet, a diaper change, an email, a pile of laundry. Ask who is on the other end of the task, and make it easier on them. Fourth, the week.
Pardon done with ihsan doesn't keep a ledger. Justice done with ihsan is gentle. Ties kept with ihsan don't wait to be repaid.
Loving for others with ihsan means the good, not just the polite. So ihsan isn't one more virtue on the list.
It's the way every virtue gets done. Not perfection. Doing the thing well, because He sees.

how: Muslims learn ihsan from the hadith of Jibril, worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and apply the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws to everyday work, including slaughter with a sharp blade and without needless suffering.

games.q: what does “excellence in all things” mean?
o: an extra good deed done only on top of what's required
being flawless in every task, never making any mistake
ihsan: doing each thing well and beautifully, as if seen

p: doing a thing beautifully and well

s: the hadith of excellence uses slaughter as its example
when you slaughter, slaughter well: sharpen the blade, spare the animal.
the hadith limits ihsan to prayer and worship
Allah has prescribed ihsan in all things.
the hadith's verb for prescribed is the fasting verse's verb
kataba: 'Fasting is prescribed for you,' al-Baqarah 2:183.

games.q: you're about to slaughter an animal for a family meal. the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws speaks to exactly this. what does it ask?
o: sharpen your blade and spare the animal suffering.
games.why: Sahih Muslim: Allah has prescribed ihsan in all things. so slaughter well: sharpen the blade, and spare the animal.

practice: Choose one ordinary task waiting for you, washing a pan, writing a reply, making the bed, and picture doing it well, not just fast: the right tool, your full attention, the last corner done.
Then ask who will meet the result, and how it could be easier on them. If you pray, you can hold the hadith of Jibril in mind: as though you see Him, and He sees you.

wordCard.voice: Excellence in all things. Ihsan: doing each thing beautifully and well, prescribed, the hadith says, right down to a sharpened blade. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: excellence, doing a thing beautifully and well.

carryVoice: Your line: excellence in everything. Written in, not extra credit. Tomorrow, the whole inward road at once.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1955 (Shaddad ibn Aws: Allah has prescribed ihsan in all things; slaughter well, sharpen the blade)
Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Jibril: ihsan is to worship Allah as though you see Him)
